title: Fiber Architecture
summary: **Fiber** is React's reimplemented reconciler (since React 16). It breaks rendering into small, interruptible units of work processed by a cooperative work loop, uses two trees (current and work-in-progress) for double buffering, and is the foundation that made concurrent features like time-slicing and Suspense possible.

subtopics.title: Reconciliation
subtopics.explanation: Reconciliation is the process of determining what changed between the previous and next UI so React can update the DOM minimally. Fiber is the reimplementation of this process: where the old 'stack' reconciler recursed synchronously and couldn't be paused, Fiber represents the same diffing work as discrete, schedulable nodes. The diffing heuristics (type-based teardown, same-type update, key-based list matching) are unchanged — Fiber changed how that work is executed, not the rules.

subtopics.title: Units of work
subtopics.explanation: A unit of work is a single fiber node React processes at a time — roughly one component instance or DOM element. Breaking rendering into small units is what lets React process a little, check whether it should yield, and either continue or hand the main thread back to the browser. This granularity is the core mechanism behind time-slicing: a long render becomes many small steps instead of one blocking task.

subtopics.title: The work loop
subtopics.explanation: The work loop is the cooperative loop that pulls one unit of work, processes it, and then checks whether it has time remaining before processing the next. If time runs low (or a higher-priority update arrives), the loop yields to the browser so it can paint and handle input, then resumes later. This cooperative scheduling — rather than a blocking recursive call stack — is what keeps the UI responsive during large updates.

subtopics.title: Interruptible rendering
subtopics.explanation: Interruptible rendering means the render phase can be paused, resumed, restarted, or abandoned entirely before anything reaches the screen. It exists so urgent updates (like typing) can preempt expensive background renders (like filtering a huge list). The major consequence for developers: because render may run more than once or never commit, render functions must be pure and side-effect-free, with effects deferred to the commit phase.

subtopics.title: Double buffering
subtopics.explanation: Double buffering is Fiber keeping two trees — the current tree reflecting what's on screen, and a work-in-progress tree built during render — with each fiber linked to its counterpart via an 'alternate' pointer. React mutates the off-screen work-in-progress tree and only swaps it to become current on commit, so an interrupted or discarded render never shows a half-finished UI. The alternate pointer lets React reuse fiber objects instead of reallocating the whole tree each render.

subtopics.title: Render vs commit
subtopics.explanation: Fiber separates an interruptible, side-effect-free render phase (build and diff the work-in-progress tree) from a synchronous, atomic commit phase (apply DOM mutations, attach refs, run effects). This separation is what makes interruptible rendering safe: all the pausable work happens before any visible change, and the actual DOM update is an indivisible step. It also explains effect timing — useLayoutEffect fires during commit before paint, useEffect after paint.

subtopics.title: Concurrent rendering
subtopics.explanation: Concurrent rendering is the set of capabilities Fiber's interruptible, prioritized model unlocks: React can prepare multiple versions of the UI at different priorities and interrupt low-priority work for urgent updates. Developers access it through useTransition (mark an update non-urgent), useDeferredValue (let a derived value lag), Suspense (pause a subtree awaiting data), and automatic batching. Importantly, Fiber improves perceived responsiveness, not raw render throughput.

foundations.overview: Fiber is the internal engine React uses to figure out what changed and update the DOM. Before Fiber, reconciliation ran in a single synchronous recursive pass that could not be paused. Fiber rewrote this as a linked structure of small work units that React can process incrementally, pause, resume, and even abandon — which is what enables React's modern concurrent features.
foundations.formalDefinition: A fiber is a JavaScript object representing a unit of work and a node in React's internal tree, roughly corresponding to a component instance or DOM element. The Fiber architecture is the reconciler that builds and processes these fiber nodes through an interruptible work loop, then commits the results to the DOM in a separate, synchronous phase.
foundations.whyItMatters: Fiber is why React can keep an app responsive during large updates: it can spread rendering work across multiple frames and let urgent updates (like typing) interrupt less urgent ones. Understanding it explains the difference between the render and commit phases and why effects, refs, and DOM mutations behave the way they do.
foundations.mentalModel: Imagine React keeping a to-do list of small tasks instead of one giant task. Each fiber is one to-do item. React works through the list a little at a time, checking the clock between items; if something more urgent comes up, it can set the list aside and come back later. When the whole list is processed it applies all the changes to the screen at once.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser has one main thread shared between JavaScript, layout, paint, and event handling. A long synchronous render blocks everything, so input feels frozen. Fiber lets React yield the main thread back to the browser between units of work, so the browser can paint and respond to input, then resume rendering when idle.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Fiber underpins every modern React app, but developers feel it directly through concurrent features: useTransition to mark updates as non-urgent, useDeferredValue to defer expensive re-renders, Suspense for streaming and async UI, and automatic batching.
foundations.businessImpact: Apps that stay responsive under heavy updates feel faster and keep users engaged; janky, frozen UIs increase abandonment. Fiber's interruptible model is what lets large React apps stay smooth.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Knowing that rendering can run more than once, be interrupted, and may not commit explains why render functions must be pure and side-effect-free, and why side effects belong in commit-phase effects rather than during render.
foundations.performanceImpact: Fiber enables time-slicing — splitting a long render into chunks so the main thread isn't blocked — and prioritization so urgent updates preempt background ones. This trades a little overhead per unit of work for far better perceived performance.
commonUseCases: Keeping typing responsive while a large list re-renders (useTransition)
Deferring an expensive derived view so the input stays snappy (useDeferredValue)
Streaming server-rendered HTML and revealing content as it loads (Suspense)
Automatic batching of multiple state updates into a single render

commonMisconceptions.myth: Fiber makes React faster at raw rendering.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Fiber adds per-unit bookkeeping; raw throughput isn't faster. Its win is responsiveness — splitting and prioritizing work so the main thread isn't blocked.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Rendering always commits to the DOM.
commonMisconceptions.reality: With Fiber the render phase can be paused, restarted, or thrown away entirely; only the commit phase actually mutates the DOM, and it runs once per committed update.

visualExplorer.title: Render phase (interruptible) vs commit phase (synchronous)
visualExplorer.caption: Watch how Fiber processes units of work in the interruptible render phase, builds a work-in-progress tree, then commits it to the DOM in one synchronous pass.

interactiveExamples.title: Render can run more than once
interactiveExamples.explanation: Because Fiber may render in the background, render functions must be pure. This example logs during render to show how often React calls it — and why you must never put side effects there.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: The render log fires on each update; the UI updates only after React commits the new tree.

interactiveExamples.title: Urgent vs non-urgent work with useTransition
interactiveExamples.explanation: Fiber can prioritize updates. Typing is urgent and stays responsive, while the expensive list build is marked as a transition so React can interrupt it to keep the input smooth.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: The input stays responsive while the large list update is processed as a lower-priority transition.

codeLab.title: Mark an expensive update as a transition
codeLab.instructions: The filter update blocks typing. Use useTransition so the input stays urgent and the expensive filtered list is computed as a non-urgent transition. Show a pending indicator while the transition runs.
codeLab.expectedOutput: Typing stays smooth; a pending indicator shows while the filtered results catch up.
hints: Keep setQuery outside the transition so typing stays urgent.
Wrap the expensive setResults call inside startTransition(() => { ... }).

debuggingLab.title: Side effect during render breaks under concurrent rendering
debuggingLab.symptom: A counter that should increment once per mount sometimes jumps by two, or logs duplicate analytics events.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Mutating external state during render assumes render runs exactly once and always commits. Under Fiber, the render phase can run multiple times, be interrupted, or be discarded — and StrictMode intentionally double-invokes render in development — so the side effect fires unpredictably.
commonMistakes: Mutating module-level or external variables during render.
Performing logging, subscriptions, or network calls in the render body.
Assuming render runs exactly once and always reaches commit.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Move the side effect out of render so it only runs after React commits, exactly once per mount.

theory.question: What is React Fiber and why was it introduced?
theory.directAnswer: Fiber is React's reconciler, rewritten in React 16. It represents rendering work as a tree of small fiber nodes, each a unit of work, processed by an interruptible work loop. It was introduced to make rendering incremental and prioritizable so React could pause, resume, or abandon work and keep the UI responsive — the foundation for concurrent features.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A reimplementation of reconciliation as a linked tree of fiber objects, each describing a unit of work, processed cooperatively rather than in one synchronous recursive pass.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The old stack reconciler recursed synchronously and could not be interrupted, so large updates blocked the main thread and froze input. Fiber lets React break work into chunks and yield to the browser.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: React walks the fiber tree creating a work-in-progress copy, processing one fiber at a time in the render phase. It checks whether it should yield between units; when complete it commits the new tree to the DOM in one synchronous pass.

theory.whyImportant: Fiber explains React's render/commit split, why render must be pure, and how concurrent features work — core advanced-interview territory.
theory.realWorldExample: When you wrap an expensive state update in useTransition, Fiber processes it at lower priority and can interrupt it so typing stays responsive.

nestedTopics.title: Stack vs Fiber reconciler
nestedTopics.explanation: The old stack reconciler used the JS call stack and was synchronous; Fiber uses its own linked structure so work can be paused and resumed.

nestedTopics.title: Unit of work
nestedTopics.explanation: Each fiber is a small chunk React can process and then decide whether to continue or yield the main thread.

nestedTopics.title: Render vs commit phases
nestedTopics.explanation: The render phase is interruptible and produces no visible change; the commit phase is synchronous and applies DOM mutations and runs effects.

followUps.question: Does Fiber change the React API you write?
followUps.answer: Mostly no — it is internal. You feel it through concurrent features like useTransition, useDeferredValue, and Suspense, and through the requirement that render stays pure.

followUps.question: Why must render functions be pure under Fiber?
followUps.answer: Because the render phase may run multiple times, be interrupted, or be discarded before commit, so any side effect there can run unexpectedly or repeatedly.

theory.question: Explain double buffering in Fiber — the current and work-in-progress trees.
theory.directAnswer: React keeps two fiber trees: the current tree, which reflects what's on screen, and a work-in-progress tree it builds during the render phase. Each fiber points to its counterpart via an 'alternate' link. When the work-in-progress tree is complete and committed, React swaps it to become the new current tree.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A double-buffering scheme where React mutates an off-screen work-in-progress tree and only swaps it in once it's fully built and committed.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Building updates on a separate tree means an in-progress render can be paused or thrown away without ever showing a half-finished UI; the user only sees complete, committed states.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: React reuses fiber objects between renders via the alternate pointer to avoid reallocating the whole tree. The render phase produces the work-in-progress tree; commit applies it and flips the current pointer.

theory.whyImportant: Double buffering is the mechanism that makes interruptible rendering safe — it's a hallmark of truly understanding Fiber.
theory.realWorldExample: An interrupted transition builds a partial work-in-progress tree; because it was never committed and never became current, the screen shows the previous consistent UI.

nestedTopics.title: Alternate pointer
nestedTopics.explanation: Each fiber links to its counterpart in the other tree so React can reuse nodes instead of recreating them.

nestedTopics.title: Tree swap on commit
nestedTopics.explanation: Committing makes the finished work-in-progress tree the new current tree in one atomic step.

followUps.question: Why two trees instead of mutating in place?
followUps.answer: Mutating in place could expose a partial UI if a render is interrupted; a separate tree guarantees the user only sees fully committed states.

scenario.question: Typing in a search box that filters a 50,000-row table is janky and laggy. Explain, in terms of Fiber, why this happens and how concurrent features fix it.
scenario.directAnswer: Each keystroke triggers a state update that, by default, is urgent — Fiber renders and commits the huge filtered list synchronously, blocking the main thread and the input. Marking the filtering update as non-urgent with useTransition (or deferring the value with useDeferredValue) lets Fiber process it at lower priority and interrupt it so keystrokes stay responsive.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A responsiveness problem caused by treating an expensive update as urgent so it monopolizes the main thread.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Without a priority hint, all updates share the highest priority; Fiber will still complete the large render before yielding, so input feels frozen.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: useTransition marks the list update as a transition. Fiber can pause the transition render to handle the urgent keystroke update, keeping the input snappy and finishing the list afterward.

scenario.whyImportant: It connects Fiber's interruptible model to a concrete performance fix interviewers love to probe.

nestedTopics.title: Update priority
nestedTopics.explanation: Fiber assigns priorities to updates; urgent ones (input) preempt transitions.

nestedTopics.title: useDeferredValue
nestedTopics.explanation: Lets a derived value lag behind so the expensive subtree re-renders at lower priority while the input stays current.

followUps.question: When would you reach for useDeferredValue instead of useTransition?
followUps.answer: Use useDeferredValue when you don't control the state setter (e.g. a value from props) and just want a derived view to render at lower priority.

coding.question: Use useDeferredValue to keep an input responsive while an expensive derived list lags behind.
coding.thoughtProcess: The input value must update urgently every keystroke. The expensive list should render from a deferred copy of that value so Fiber can render it at lower priority. I read the live value into the input and the deferred value into the list, and detect staleness by comparing them.
coding.lineByLine: query holds the live, urgent input value. useDeferredValue(query) returns a copy that Fiber may let lag behind. The list filters from deferredQuery so the heavy work runs at lower priority. Comparing query to deferredQuery detects the stale frame so we can dim the output while it catches up.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) per committed list render in the number of rows; the input update itself is O(1).
coding.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the filtered results array.

alternativeApproaches.title: useTransition
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Wrap the setter in startTransition when you own the state update. useDeferredValue is preferable when you only have the value, not the setter.

followUps.question: Does useDeferredValue debounce the input?
followUps.answer: No. It doesn't add a fixed delay; Fiber renders the deferred value at lower priority and may interrupt it, so it adapts to how busy the main thread is.

systemDesign.question: Design the rendering architecture of a UI library that must stay responsive during large updates. What does Fiber's design teach you about the key decisions?
systemDesign.directAnswer: Separate computing the next UI (render) from applying it (commit); make the render phase incremental and interruptible by representing work as small units; keep two trees so an interrupted render never shows a partial UI; and assign priorities so urgent input can preempt background work. These are exactly the choices Fiber makes.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An architecture that turns rendering into schedulable, prioritizable, interruptible work with an atomic commit, rather than one blocking synchronous pass.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Browsers run UI work on a single main thread, so any long synchronous task freezes input and animation. Incremental, prioritized work keeps the thread free for urgent events.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Model each component as a unit of work in a linked tree; run a work loop that processes units and yields to the browser when time runs low; build a work-in-progress tree via double buffering; commit it atomically; and tag updates with priorities so a scheduler can preempt low-priority work.

systemDesign.whyImportant: It shows you can reason about scheduling, main-thread constraints, and consistency guarantees — the architectural thinking Fiber embodies.

nestedTopics.title: Cooperative scheduling
nestedTopics.explanation: Yield the main thread between units of work so the browser can paint and handle input, then resume.

nestedTopics.title: Phase separation
nestedTopics.explanation: An interruptible, side-effect-free render phase plus a synchronous, atomic commit phase keeps updates consistent.

nestedTopics.title: Priority lanes
nestedTopics.explanation: Tagging updates with priorities lets a scheduler interrupt low-priority renders for urgent ones.

followUps.question: What are the trade-offs of this design?
followUps.answer: More bookkeeping and complexity per unit of work, and render code must be pure and repeatable; in exchange you get responsiveness, prioritization, and the ability to abandon work safely.

followUps.question: How does this enable Suspense?
followUps.answer: Because render can pause and the work-in-progress tree isn't committed until ready, React can suspend a subtree awaiting data and show a fallback without breaking the visible UI.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Fiber splits work into a schedulable render phase and an atomic commit phase, with two trees (current and work-in-progress) connected by alternate pointers. Design app code around this: pure render, side effects in effects, and priority hints (useTransition/useDeferredValue) for expensive updates.
productionDeepDive.performance: The win is responsiveness via time-slicing and prioritization, not raw render speed. Profile with React DevTools' Profiler to find long renders, then split components and mark non-urgent updates as transitions so the main thread stays free.
productionDeepDive.security: Fiber is internal and doesn't change the security model; the usual rules apply — never trust user-controlled state in render output without sanitization, and avoid dangerouslySetInnerHTML with untrusted data.
productionDeepDive.scaling: As trees grow, Fiber's incremental rendering keeps large apps responsive, but deep trees and frequent updates still cost work. Memoization, list virtualization, and transitions keep big screens smooth.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Embracing the render/commit split — pure render, effects for side effects — keeps components predictable under concurrent rendering and StrictMode's double-invocation, which surfaces impure code early.
productionDeepDive.observability: React DevTools' Profiler visualizes render phases, flame graphs, and why each component rendered; StrictMode double-invokes render and effects in development to expose side effects that Fiber's repeatable rendering would otherwise punish.

caseStudies.problem: Typing into a filter over a huge list froze the UI because each keystroke synchronously re-rendered everything.
caseStudies.solution: Marked the list update as a transition with useTransition so Fiber rendered it at lower priority and could interrupt it for keystrokes.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Results lag slightly behind input and need a pending indicator, but typing stays smooth.
caseStudies.lessons: Lean on Fiber's prioritization for expensive updates instead of fighting the main thread.

projectBuilder.summary: Build a search-over-large-dataset UI that stays responsive by leveraging Fiber's concurrent features, then observe render behavior with the Profiler.
requirements: A search input that filters a large generated dataset (10k+ rows)
A results view that updates at lower priority than the input
A visible pending/stale indicator while results catch up
projectBuilder.architecture: Hold the live query in state for the urgent input. Derive the heavy filtered list from a deferred value (useDeferredValue) or update it inside startTransition so Fiber can interrupt that render to keep input responsive. Keep render pure and put any logging in effects.

steps.title: Generate the dataset
steps.instructions: Create a large in-memory array of rows to make rendering measurably expensive.
steps.checkpoint: Typing without optimization is visibly janky in the Profiler.

steps.title: Make the input urgent
steps.instructions: Keep the input value in state and read the deferred value for filtering with useDeferredValue.
steps.checkpoint: The input stays responsive while results lag slightly.

steps.title: Add a stale indicator
steps.instructions: Compare the live and deferred values to detect staleness and dim the results while they update.
steps.checkpoint: A pending state shows during heavy updates.

steps.instructions: Use the React DevTools Profiler to confirm render work is happening at lower priority and not blocking input.
steps.checkpoint: Flame graphs show input updates committing ahead of the heavy list render.

Swap useDeferredValue for useTransition where you own the setter and compare the developer experience

How do Fiber's render and commit phases explain when your effects and DOM updates run?

keyTakeaways: Fiber is React's reconciler (since v16): rendering is a tree of small, interruptible units of work processed by a cooperative work loop.
Fiber separates an interruptible render phase (no visible changes, must be pure) from a synchronous commit phase (DOM mutations and effects).
Double buffering uses two trees — current (on screen) and work-in-progress (being built) — linked by alternate pointers and swapped atomically on commit.
Because render can run multiple times, pause, or be discarded, render functions must be pure and side-effect-free.
Fiber's interruptibility and prioritization are what enable concurrent features: useTransition, useDeferredValue, Suspense, and automatic batching.
Fiber improves responsiveness (time-slicing, priority), not raw render throughput.
